extracted.intended_audience: patent scholars, patent examiners, IP policymakers, and practitioners evaluating patent quality
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Edmund Kitch's 'prospect theory' to evaluate the functional quality of a patent: whether it efficiently coordinates post‑grant development by staking a clear, enabled, and appropriately scoped technological prospect at the right time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early Issuance
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent should be granted early in the development cycle of the technology, before substantial commercial investment is made by competitors. Late-issued patents on already-developed prospects fail the coordination function and impose pure deadweight cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing is crucial: a patent that issues after significant duplicative investment cannot perform the prospect-coordination function and merely redistributes or destroys value. Examiners and evaluators should consider whether the priority/filing/issuance timing allowed the patent to serve as a stake for subsequent coordinated development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad but Bounded Scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims should reach all natural extensions and improvements of the prospect that a rational developer would coordinate, but no further. Scope should match the technological field that the inventor's disclosure reasonably enables further investigation of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good claim scope captures the practical prospect (including foreseeable variants) while avoiding overreaching beyond what the disclosure and contribution justify. Evaluate whether claim breadth maps to realistic coordination needs rather than speculative monopolization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definite Boundaries (Notice Function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim boundaries must be sufficiently clear that subsequent investors can identify the prospect and either (a) negotiate a license, (b) design around, or (c) develop within the prospect under the patentee's coordination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definiteness serves the notice function—claims should enable competent third parties to determine whether planned activity falls within the prospect. Ambiguous boundaries undermine negotiation, design-around, and coordinated development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure Sufficient to Enable Further Investment
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must disclose enough technical content that subsequent improvers can build on the disclosure. Kitch criticizes patents whose disclosure is so thin that no real 'prospect' is staked—these patents fail to perform the informational coordination function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the written disclosure lets others meaningfully evaluate and invest in developing the disclosed prospect; thin, paper disclosures that do not enable follow-on work are defective under the prospect standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims map to the identified technological problem
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims map directly onto the technological problem the inventor identified, not onto incidental embodiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred drafting aligns claim scope with the problem addressed by the inventor, avoiding fixation on particular embodiments that do not reflect the real prospect. This supports coherent coordination of subsequent development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification anticipates and discloses obvious further development
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification anticipates and discloses the obvious lines of further development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong prospect-patent explains likely next steps and improvements so that potential developers understand the prospect's boundaries and development pathways; this is an enabling/informational virtue rather than overclaiming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of functional or generic claim language when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim language uses functional or generic terms where the prospect properly extends to functionally equivalent embodiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the prospect legitimately covers functional equivalents, drafting in functional/generic terms helps capture the coordinated field without artificial embodiment limits; but this must be supported by disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claims trace concrete embodiments without artificially narrowing the prospect
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependent claims trace concrete embodiments without artificially narrowing the prospect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependent claims should document specific embodiments while preserving the inventor's broader prospect; they should not be used to constrict the practical coordination space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that exceed disclosure without explanation ('paper claims')
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims dramatically exceed the disclosed embodiments without explaining why the prospect is broader (signal: 'paper claims' without working examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an anti-pattern: broad claims unsupported by disclosure fail the prospect function by asserting rights to a non-staked prospect. Such claims should be scrutinized for enablement and written-description shortcomings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessively narrow claims (wasteful duplication risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are excessively narrow, leaving the surrounding prospect open to wasteful duplicative investment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overly narrow claims may fail to coordinate development, allowing multiple parties to duplicate efforts inefficiently. Evaluate whether claim narrowness undermines the system's coordination purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withholding specification information to preserve litigation positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification withholds information that would allow rational coordination (deliberate ambiguity to support later litigation positions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate vagueness or strategic nondisclosure that prevents third parties from evaluating or investing in the prospect is a defect under the prospect framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent issues too late for prospect-coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent issues so late that prospect-coordination is impossible (no notice value to subsequent developers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A late-issued patent cannot supply the informational/coordination benefits Kitch attributes to good patents; timing relative to industry investment is a critical evaluative factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press applicants for early disclosure of the technological prospect
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should press applicants for early disclosure of the technological prospect, not merely the embodiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner practice that elicits a full prospect disclosure (anticipated developments, variants, and functional scope) produces patents better suited for coordinating post-grant investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject claims that exceed the inventor's actual prospect (enablement/written description)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject claims so broad that they exceed the inventor's actual prospect (enablement, written description).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner rejections grounded in enablement and written-description doctrine serve the prospect aim by preventing overbroad, non-enabled monopolies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject claims so narrow they fail to define a coordinated prospect
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject claims so narrow that they fail to define a coordinated prospect (utility of the patent system itself).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should avoid allowing claims that are functionally useless for coordination; the patent must be useful for organizing follow-on development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand definite claim boundaries enforceable under 35 U.S.C. 112(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Demand definite boundaries that subsequent investors can rely upon (35 U.S.C. 112(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definiteness requirements operationalize the notice function; examiners should ensure claims give third parties adequate notice of scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination potential
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the claim define a discrete prospect that one entity could rationally coordinate?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claimed invention and disclosure create a natural unit of development that a single firm or licensor could organize, rather than fragmenting rights or leaving coordination to costly bargaining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Could a competent third-party investor read the claims and know whether their planned activity falls within the prospect?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the operational test of definiteness from the investor/developer perspective: clarity enables licensing, design-around, or coordinated development decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure completeness for prospect
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the specification disclose enough that the prospect can be developed by the patentee or licensees?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess completeness with an eye toward enabling follow-on development activities and lowering the information asymmetry between patentee and potential developers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing (was the prospect staked early?)
rubrics_metrics.description: Was the prospect staked before substantial duplicative investment?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider filing and issuance timing relative to industry activity; early staking is essential for the patent to perform its coordination and notice roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope-disclosure match
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the breadth of the claims correspond to the breadth of the inventor's actual technological contribution?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good patent's claim breadth should be justified by the disclosure and the inventor's contribution—neither overreaching nor artificially narrow relative to the enabled prospect.
